content.stem: Magnetic particle testing can be used only on materials that are:
content.explanation: MT relies on a part holding a magnetic field and forming leakage fields at discontinuities. Only ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt and many of their alloys) can be magnetized strongly enough to do this.
distractors: Paramagnetic materials are only very weakly attracted to a field and cannot retain or concentrate flux enough to form usable leakage fields.
Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled by a field and cannot be magnetized for MT.
Conductivity governs eddy-current and some other methods, not whether a part can be magnetized; austenitic stainless is conductive but non-ferromagnetic.

content.stem: Magnetic poles of opposite polarity placed near each other will:
content.explanation: Unlike poles attract; like poles repel. Leakage fields at a crack act as local north and south poles that attract magnetic particles.
distractors: Repulsion occurs between like poles, not opposite poles.
Opposite poles exert a real attractive force, not a neutral one.
Opposite poles do not cancel; the field between them is reinforced along the path connecting them.

content.stem: Magnetic flux lines outside a bar magnet travel from:
options: The center outward in all directions
content.explanation: By convention, flux lines emerge from the north pole, travel through the surrounding medium to the south pole, and continue north to south inside the magnet, forming closed loops.
distractors: South-to-north is the internal direction of the lines inside the magnet, not the external path.
Lines run between opposite poles; they do not connect a pole to another of the same polarity.
Flux lines are organized loops between poles, not a uniform radial spray from the center.

content.stem: A surface crack produces an indication in MT because it:
options: Distorts the field and creates a flux leakage field above the surface
Increases the permeability of the part locally
Heats the particles so they adhere
content.explanation: A discontinuity interrupts the flow of flux in the part. Flux is forced out of the surface, creating a local leakage field with north and south poles that hold magnetic particles, forming a visible indication.
distractors: A crack is essentially an air gap; it lowers permeability locally, which is why flux leaks out rather than passing through.
MT is not a thermal process; particle adherence is magnetic, not heat driven.
Particles are held by magnetic attraction at the leakage field, not by electrical conduction.

content.stem: Magnetic permeability of a material is best described as:
options: The ease with which it can be magnetized
Its ability to retain magnetism after the force is removed
The force needed to remove residual magnetism
Its electrical resistance to current flow
content.explanation: Permeability is the ratio of flux density (B) to magnetizing force (H). A high-permeability material is magnetized easily by a given force.
distractors: Retention of magnetism after the force is removed is retentivity, not permeability.
The force needed to remove residual magnetism is coercive force (coercivity), not permeability.
Resistance to current is electrical resistivity and is unrelated to magnetic permeability.

content.stem: Retentivity of a ferromagnetic material refers to its ability to:
options: Retain residual magnetism after the magnetizing force is removed
Be magnetized easily by a small force
content.explanation: Retentivity is the amount of residual flux a material holds once the applied magnetizing force is removed. High-retentivity materials are suited to the residual technique.
distractors: Ease of magnetization by a small force describes permeability.
Resistance to becoming magnetized relates to low permeability, not retentivity.
Current carrying is an electrical property, not a magnetic one.

content.stem: The magnetism remaining in a part after the magnetizing force is removed is called:
content.explanation: Residual magnetism is the flux retained by the part after the current or applied field is shut off. It is the basis of the residual inspection technique.
distractors: Coercive force is the reverse field needed to bring the residual flux back to zero.
Reluctance is the opposition of a magnetic circuit to the establishment of flux, analogous to resistance.
Permeance is the reciprocal of reluctance, not the leftover field.

content.stem: Coercive force is the:
options: Reverse magnetizing force required to remove residual magnetism
Force that magnetizes a part to saturation
Force holding particles to a leakage field
Field strength at the surface of the part
content.explanation: Coercive force (coercivity) is the magnetizing force of opposite polarity needed to reduce residual flux density in the part to zero. High coercivity makes a part harder to demagnetize.
distractors: The force that drives a part toward saturation is simply the applied magnetizing force, not coercive force specifically.
Particle adherence is due to the leakage field, unrelated to coercive force.
Surface field strength is measured in gauss; it is not the definition of coercive force.

content.stem: Reluctance in a magnetic circuit is analogous to which quantity in an electrical circuit?
content.explanation: Reluctance opposes the establishment of magnetic flux just as resistance opposes the flow of current. Flux corresponds to current and magnetomotive force corresponds to voltage.
distractors: Voltage corresponds to magnetomotive force, the driving cause, not the opposition.
Current corresponds to magnetic flux, the quantity that flows, not the opposition to it.
Capacitance has no direct magnetic-circuit analog in this comparison.

content.stem: On a hysteresis (B-H) curve, the point where flux density (B) no longer increases with increasing magnetizing force (H) is called:
content.explanation: At saturation the material's magnetic domains are essentially fully aligned, so further increases in H produce little or no increase in B.
distractors: Retentivity is the B value remaining when H returns to zero, read on the vertical axis.
Coercive force is the H value needed to return B to zero, read on the horizontal axis.
There is no standard point called the knee of permeability on the hysteresis loop in this context.

content.stem: When current passes through a straight conductor, the magnetic field around it is:
options: Circular and perpendicular to the conductor
Longitudinal and parallel to the conductor
Radial, pointing away from the conductor
Present only at the ends of the conductor
content.explanation: A current-carrying conductor produces a circular magnetic field that encircles the conductor in planes perpendicular to it. This is the basis of circular magnetization.
distractors: A longitudinal field parallel to the axis is produced by a coil, not by a straight current-carrying conductor.
The field encircles the conductor; it does not radiate straight outward.
The circular field exists along the entire length of the conductor, not just at the ends.

content.stem: The right-hand rule for a current-carrying conductor relates the direction of current flow to the:
options: Direction of the encircling magnetic field
content.explanation: With the thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current, the curled fingers show the direction of the circular magnetic field around the conductor.
distractors: The rule gives field direction, not field strength.
End polarity is associated with longitudinal (coil) magnetization, not the circular field of a straight conductor.
Penetration depth depends on current type and frequency, not the right-hand rule.

content.stem: Circular magnetization of a part produces a magnetic field that is oriented:
options: Around the circumference, perpendicular to the current path
Along the length of the part between two poles
Only on the inside surface of a hollow part
content.explanation: Passing current through the part (or through a central conductor) sets up a circular field around the part. Best detection is of discontinuities parallel to the current, i.e., longitudinal/axial cracks.
distractors: A field along the length between poles describes longitudinal magnetization from a coil or yoke.
The circular field encircles the part; it does not radiate outward.
With a central conductor the circular field appears on both inside and outside surfaces of a hollow part.

content.stem: Longitudinal magnetization sets up a field that runs:
options: Lengthwise through the part, creating poles at the ends
Around the circumference of the part
In a spiral along the surface
Only at the exact center of the part
content.explanation: A coil or yoke induces a longitudinal field along the part's length, producing north and south poles at the ends. It best detects discontinuities transverse to that field.
distractors: A circumferential field is the result of circular magnetization, not longitudinal.
A simple coil or yoke produces a lengthwise field, not a spiral.
The longitudinal field runs through the whole part, not only the center.

content.stem: A discontinuity is most readily detected when its principal plane is:
options: Perpendicular (about 45 to 90 degrees) to the magnetic field
Aligned exactly with the current flow only
At any angle, since orientation does not matter
content.explanation: Maximum flux leakage occurs when a discontinuity lies across the field. Detectability falls off as the angle decreases; below roughly 45 degrees indications become weak or are missed.
distractors: A discontinuity parallel to the field causes little flux disturbance and may produce no indication.
Cracks parallel to current (perpendicular to the circular field) are exactly the ones a circular field finds; the statement confuses current and field orientation.
Orientation matters greatly; this is why parts are magnetized in two perpendicular directions.

content.stem: To detect discontinuities in all orientations, a part should be magnetized:
options: In at least two perpendicular directions
content.explanation: Because indications form best across the field, a single field direction leaves cracks parallel to it undetected. Two perpendicular shots (or a multidirectional technique) cover all orientations.
distractors: A single direction misses discontinuities aligned with the field.
Longitudinal alone misses longitudinal/axial cracks.
Circular alone misses transverse/circumferential cracks.

content.stem: Flux density (B) is expressed in which units in the CGS system commonly used in MT?
content.explanation: Flux density B in the CGS system is measured in gauss. Magnetizing force H is measured in oersteds. Field indicators such as gaussmeters read in gauss.
distractors: Amperes measure current, not flux density.
Oersteds measure magnetizing force H, not flux density B.
Webers per second describe a rate of flux change (voltage), not steady flux density.

content.stem: In a ferromagnetic material, magnetization occurs as applied force causes:
options: Magnetic domains to align with the field
The material to become electrically charged
Atoms to physically migrate through the metal
The crystal lattice to expand permanently
content.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials contain magnetic domains. Under an applied field, domains aligned with the field grow and rotate into alignment, increasing net magnetization until saturation.
distractors: Magnetization is not an electrostatic charging of the material.
Atoms do not migrate; only the alignment of domain magnetization changes.
Magnetization does not cause permanent lattice expansion.

content.stem: Above its Curie temperature, a ferromagnetic material:
content.explanation: At the Curie point thermal agitation overcomes domain alignment and the material becomes paramagnetic, losing the ferromagnetism needed for MT until it cools below that temperature.
distractors: It loses magnetism above the Curie point rather than becoming permanently magnetized.
Permeability collapses toward that of a paramagnet; it does not double.
Conductivity is not what changes; the magnetic ordering is lost.

content.stem: Compared with the field from a coil, the circular field from passing current through a part is generally:
options: Contained largely within and around the part with no external poles
Unable to detect any surface cracks
content.explanation: A circular field is self-contained around the current path and produces no free external poles, so parts magnetized circularly hold little external leakage except at discontinuities. A coil produces strong external poles at the ends.
distractors: The circular field is typically strong at the surface where current density is highest, especially with AC.
Circular fields are produced with both AC and DC current.
Circular magnetization readily detects longitudinal surface cracks; it is a primary technique.

content.stem: A material with high magnetic permeability will:
options: Reach a given flux density with relatively little magnetizing force
Require a very large force to reach any flux density
content.explanation: High permeability means a large change in B for a small change in H, so the part magnetizes readily. Permeability and retentivity are distinct properties.
distractors: Needing a very large force describes low permeability.
High permeability does not guarantee high retentivity; soft magnetic materials can be highly permeable yet retain little.
Ease of demagnetization relates to coercivity; high permeability does not make a part impossible to demagnetize.

content.stem: A magnetically 'soft' material, compared with a magnetically 'hard' material, typically has:
options: Low retentivity and low coercive force
High retentivity and high coercive force
No response to a magnetic field
content.explanation: Soft magnetic materials (e.g., low-carbon steels) magnetize and demagnetize easily, with low retentivity and coercivity. Hard materials (e.g., high-carbon, hardened steels) retain magnetism strongly.
distractors: High retentivity and coercive force describe magnetically hard materials.
Soft materials have high permeability and low reluctance, the opposite of this option.
Soft materials respond readily to a field; only the ease of retaining it is low.

content.stem: The strength of the leakage field at a surface crack increases as the crack becomes:
options: Deeper and more perpendicular to the field
Shallower and more parallel to the field
content.explanation: A deeper crack interrupts more flux, and one perpendicular to the field maximizes the disturbance, so both increase leakage-field strength and indication contrast.
distractors: Shallow cracks parallel to the field produce weak leakage and are easily missed.
Width alone does not maximize leakage; a tight, deep, transverse crack leaks strongly.
A crack filled with conductive (ferromagnetic) material would carry flux and leak less.

content.stem: Compared with a surface-breaking crack at the same depth, a subsurface discontinuity produces a leakage field that is:
options: Weaker and more spread out at the surface
content.explanation: Flux leakage must travel farther to reach the surface from a subsurface defect, so the field is weaker and broader. This is why subsurface detection needs higher fields and dry powder or HWDC.
distractors: Subsurface indications are weaker and fuzzier, not stronger and sharper.
The leakage from a buried defect differs markedly from a surface-breaking one.
Polarity is not reversed; only strength and definition change.

content.stem: In a solid bar magnetized circularly by passing current through it, the magnetic field strength is:
options: Zero at the center and maximum at the surface
Maximum at the center and zero at the surface
content.explanation: For a solid cylindrical conductor, the internal circular field rises from zero on the axis to a maximum at the surface. Detection is therefore strongest at and near the surface.
distractors: The field is zero on the axis, not maximum there.
The field is not uniform; it varies with radius across the section.
The circular field is present along the length, not concentrated at the ends.

content.stem: Magnetomotive force in a coil is the product of:
options: The number of turns and the current (ampere-turns)
content.explanation: MMF = N x I, the ampere-turns of the coil, is the driving force that establishes flux. This is why coil formulas are written in terms of NI.
distractors: Voltage times resistance is not the definition of MMF.
Flux density times area gives total flux, not the driving force.
Reluctance times flux gives MMF; reluctance times permeability is not meaningful here.

content.stem: A longitudinal field in a shaft is best suited to find discontinuities that are:
content.explanation: A longitudinal field runs along the axis, so it best reveals discontinuities lying across that field, which on a shaft are the transverse/circumferential ones.
distractors: Axial cracks lie parallel to a longitudinal field and are better found with a circular field.
The field detects transverse cracks anywhere along the length, not just the ends.
Longitudinal magnetization is not limited to the inside diameter.

content.stem: Magnetizing a part well beyond saturation is undesirable mainly because it:
options: Produces excessive field with little gain and heavy background, and can be hard to demagnetize
Converts surface cracks to subsurface ones
content.explanation: Past saturation, extra current adds little detectability but increases particle background (furring), part heating, arc-burn risk with prods, and residual field that complicates demagnetization.
distractors: Excess field does not reverse indication polarity.
Field strength does not relocate cracks within the material.
Overmagnetizing tends to leave more residual magnetism, not eliminate it.

content.stem: Magnetic flux tends to follow the path of:
content.explanation: Flux concentrates in the path of least reluctance, just as current favors least resistance. A crack (air gap) is high reluctance, forcing flux to leak around it toward the surface.
distractors: Flux avoids high-reluctance paths; it does not seek them.
Electrical resistance governs current, not the flux path.
Flux favors high permeability (low reluctance), not low permeability.

content.stem: Magnetizing force (H), the field intensity applied to a part, is expressed in:
content.explanation: H, the applied field intensity, is measured in oersteds in the CGS system (or ampere-turns per meter in SI). B, the resulting flux density, is in gauss.
distractors: Gauss is the unit of flux density B, not magnetizing force H.
Webers measure total magnetic flux, not field intensity.
Henrys measure inductance, not magnetizing force.

content.stem: Magnetic particles are attracted to a discontinuity because the discontinuity acts like:
options: A small magnet with north and south poles
content.explanation: Flux leaking out at the discontinuity forms local north and south poles. Particles bridge these poles, building a visible indication.
distractors: There is no thermal mechanism; attraction is magnetic.
Particles are not attracted by grounding or current flow at the indication.
Fluorescence under UV makes wet fluorescent indications visible but is not why particles gather there.

content.stem: When a part is magnetized by an external field without direct current contact, the field in the part is said to be:
content.explanation: Indirect (induced) magnetization uses a coil, yoke, or central conductor to induce a field in the part without passing current through the part itself. Direct magnetization passes current through the part.
distractors: Direct magnetization passes current through the part via contacts, which this does not.
Induced fields can be applied continuously; they are not limited to the residual condition.
Induced fields can be longitudinal (coil/yoke) or circular (central conductor), not only circular.

content.stem: Demagnetization of a part is accomplished by subjecting it to a field that is:
options: Reversing in direction while gradually decreasing in strength
content.explanation: Cycling the field through diminishing reversals walks the material down successive hysteresis loops toward zero residual flux. A steady or growing field would only re-magnetize it.
distractors: A steadily increasing one-direction field magnetizes rather than demagnetizes.
A strong constant field magnetizes the part further.
A zero field does nothing to remove existing residual magnetism.

content.stem: Detecting a fine subsurface discontinuity generally requires, compared with a surface crack:
content.explanation: Because subsurface leakage fields are weak and broad, higher field strengths (and dry powder or HWDC) are needed to raise enough leakage to the surface to form an indication.
distractors: A weaker field would fail to bring subsurface leakage to the surface.
MT always requires a magnetizing field.
The residual technique is generally less sensitive and poorly suited to subsurface defects.

content.stem: A ring-shaped part magnetized circularly by a central conductor will:
options: Hold a field with no external poles unless a discontinuity is present
Have strong north and south poles on its outer rim
Be impossible to inspect on the inner diameter
content.explanation: A toroidal circular field is fully contained within the ring, so there are no free external poles. A discontinuity is what locally creates poles and an indication; the central conductor inspects both ID and OD.
distractors: A circular field produces no free external poles on a sound ring.
The central conductor technique is specifically good for inspecting the inner diameter.
The part retains residual field per its retentivity; it does not lose magnetism instantly.

content.stem: On the initial magnetization (virgin) curve, the ratio B/H at any point represents the material's:
content.explanation: Permeability equals B divided by H. Along the magnetization curve this ratio changes, rising to a maximum and then falling as the material approaches saturation.
distractors: Coercive force is a specific H value at B = 0 on the descending loop, not the B/H ratio.
Retentivity is the B value at H = 0, not the ratio.
Reluctance is a magnetic-circuit property, not the point-by-point B/H ratio of the material.

content.stem: The general rule for reliable detection is that the magnetic field should be oriented:
options: As close to perpendicular to the expected discontinuity as practical
At 30 degrees or less to the discontinuity
In line with the part's long axis only
content.explanation: Indications are strongest when the field crosses the discontinuity. Practice limits acceptable angles to roughly 45 to 90 degrees between field and defect.
distractors: A field parallel to the discontinuity gives little or no indication.
Angles of 30 degrees or less produce weak, unreliable indications.
Restricting the field to the long axis would miss axial discontinuities.

content.stem: Which combination most increases flux leakage at a discontinuity?
options: A tight, deep crack oriented across a strong field at the surface
A wide, shallow crack parallel to a weak field
A subsurface void in a low field
A rounded inclusion aligned with the field
content.explanation: Leakage is greatest for a near-surface, deep, tight discontinuity lying across a strong field. Depth and perpendicular orientation interrupt the most flux.
distractors: A shallow crack parallel to a weak field leaks very little.
A deep subsurface void in a weak field produces only faint, broad leakage.
A rounded inclusion aligned with the field disturbs flux minimally.

content.stem: Doubling the current through a straight conductor, with everything else unchanged, will:
options: Approximately double the surrounding field strength
Have no effect on the field
content.explanation: Field strength around a conductor is proportional to the current. Doubling the current roughly doubles the encircling field for a given distance.
distractors: Increasing current increases, not decreases, the field.
Current directly controls field strength, so a change has a clear effect.
Reversing direction requires reversing current polarity, not increasing magnitude.

content.stem: Austenitic stainless steel is generally unsuitable for MT because it is:
content.explanation: Most austenitic stainless steels are nonferromagnetic and cannot form usable leakage fields, so MT does not apply. Penetrant or other methods are used instead.
distractors: The problem is the absence of ferromagnetism, not excessive retentivity.
Conductivity is not the disqualifier; the lack of ferromagnetism is.
Section thickness is not the issue; the alloy simply will not magnetize.

content.stem: In direct magnetization, the magnetizing current is:
content.explanation: Direct magnetization passes current through the part (head shot or prods), establishing a circular field. Indirect methods induce a field without current in the part.
distractors: A coil induces a field without current through the part; that is indirect magnetization.
A central conductor carries current near, not through, the part; that is indirect.
A permanent magnet induces a field without current through the part.

content.stem: Clamping a part between the head and tailstock contacts and passing current through it is called a:
content.explanation: A head shot passes current directly through the part end to end, producing a circular field for detecting longitudinal discontinuities.
distractors: A coil shot induces a longitudinal field; it does not pass current through the part.
A central conductor passes current through a bar inside a hollow part, not through the part.
A yoke induces a longitudinal field between two poles with no current in the part.

content.stem: Circular magnetization is best for detecting discontinuities that are:
options: At 45 degrees to the surface only
content.explanation: The circular field encircles the current path, so it crosses discontinuities lying parallel to the current, i.e., longitudinal/axial cracks, giving the strongest indications for those.
distractors: Transverse discontinuities lie along the circular field and are better found longitudinally.
Detectability is not limited to a single 45-degree orientation.
Circular magnetization detects surface discontinuities well, not only subsurface.

content.stem: A coil (solenoid) shot is used primarily to detect discontinuities oriented:
options: Parallel to the part's long axis
content.explanation: A coil produces a longitudinal field, so it best reveals transverse/circumferential discontinuities that lie across the field.
distractors: Axial discontinuities lie along the longitudinal field and are better found with a circular shot.
The coil field is not limited to the inside diameter.
Coil magnetization is general, not restricted to weld toes.

content.stem: Prods are used to produce a localized:
options: Circular field between the two prod tips
Longitudinal field along the whole part
content.explanation: Current passing between two prod tips creates a circular field in the region between and around them, useful for large castings, weldments, and structures.
distractors: A whole-part longitudinal field comes from a coil or yoke, not prods.
Prods are for solid and surface areas; central conductors handle hollow part IDs.
Prods are typically used with the continuous technique, not as a residual method.

content.stem: The principal hazard associated with the prod technique is:
options: Arc burns (local overheating) at the prod contact points
content.explanation: Poor contact, high current, or lifting prods under load can cause arcing and local burns or microstructural damage, which is unacceptable on many finished or critical surfaces.
distractors: UV exposure is a fluorescent-lighting concern, not a prod-specific hazard.
Bath contamination is unrelated to the prod electrical contact hazard.
Arc burn, not loss of residual field, is the prod hazard.

content.stem: Recommended prod spacing for typical inspection is generally:
content.explanation: Prod spacing is commonly kept between roughly 2 and 8 inches. Too close crowds the field; too far weakens it and leaves gaps in coverage.
distractors: Spacing under 1 inch concentrates the field too tightly and is impractical for coverage.
Spacing of 12 to 18 inches is too wide; field strength between prods drops off.
Spacing strongly affects field strength and coverage, so it does matter.

content.stem: To inspect the inside and outside surfaces of a hollow cylinder for longitudinal cracks, the best method is:
options: A central conductor through the bore
Prods on the outer surface only
content.explanation: A central conductor carries current through the bore, producing a circular field on both ID and OD without contact marks, ideal for tubes, rings, and pipe.
distractors: A coil gives a longitudinal field and finds transverse cracks, not longitudinal ones.
A yoke gives a localized longitudinal field, again better for transverse defects.
Prods would mark the surface and would not inspect the inside diameter.

content.stem: When a central conductor does not fill the bore, inspection of a large-diameter ring is done by:
options: Positioning the conductor against the bore wall and rotating the part in steps
Centering the conductor and inspecting only once
Doubling the current and inspecting once
content.explanation: An offset (non-filling) central conductor produces an adequate field only in the bore region nearest it (about four conductor diameters), so the part is rotated and re-inspected in overlapping segments.
distractors: A single centered shot will not give adequate field over the whole circumference if the conductor does not fill the bore.
Simply doubling current does not solve the non-uniform field of an offset conductor.
Residual magnetization does not address the offset-conductor coverage problem.

content.stem: In the continuous (true continuous) technique, the magnetic particles are applied:
options: While the magnetizing current is on
Only after the current is shut off
content.explanation: In the continuous technique the field is energized while particles are applied and allowed to gather, then current is shut off. It is more sensitive and is the most common technique.
distractors: Applying particles only after current is off describes the residual technique.
Particles are applied after cleaning, and timing relative to current, not cleaning, defines the technique.
Particle application is part of inspection, not demagnetization.

content.stem: The residual technique relies on:
options: The part's retained field after the current is removed
Particles applied during the current shot
A permanent magnet held against the part
content.explanation: In the residual technique the part is magnetized, current removed, then particles applied, using only the residual field. It suits materials with high retentivity.
distractors: Applying particles during the shot is the continuous technique.
The residual technique uses the part's own retained field, not a held permanent magnet.
Continuous AC during application is, by definition, the continuous technique.

content.stem: The residual technique is appropriate only when the material has:
content.explanation: Residual inspection needs the part to hold a strong residual field after the force is removed, so it requires adequate retentivity (typically harder steels).
distractors: Low-retentivity (soft) materials lose the field and give weak or no residual indications.
Nonferromagnetic materials cannot be inspected by MT at all.
Conductivity does not determine residual-technique suitability; retentivity does.

content.stem: Compared with the residual technique, the continuous technique generally provides:
options: Greater sensitivity to fine and subsurface discontinuities
Indications only on the inside diameter
No need for proper field direction
content.explanation: Because the field is at full strength while particles gather, the continuous technique gives stronger leakage and better sensitivity, especially for fine or subsurface defects.
distractors: The continuous technique is more sensitive, not less.
It is not restricted to the inside diameter.
Correct field direction is required regardless of technique.

content.stem: Multidirectional (multi-vector) magnetization detects discontinuities in multiple orientations by:
options: Rapidly alternating two or more fields so their combined vector sweeps directions
Using a single steady DC field
Applying particles only after all current is off
Magnetizing the part once in one axis
content.explanation: Multidirectional units energize two or more circuits in rapid sequence so the resultant field direction cycles, revealing discontinuities of differing orientations in one operation. It requires verification of adequate field in each direction.
distractors: A single steady DC field covers only one orientation.
Multidirectional magnetization is a continuous technique with current on during application.
Single-axis magnetization is exactly what multidirectional is designed to avoid.

content.stem: Adequate field balance in a multidirectional setup is commonly verified using:
options: A QQI (artificial flaw) shim showing indications in all required directions
A single gaussmeter reading at one point
content.explanation: QQI shims placed at critical locations must show clear indications in every required direction, confirming the combined fields are balanced and adequate. A single gauss reading cannot confirm all directions.
distractors: One gaussmeter reading checks one direction at one point, not the balance of all fields.
Bath concentration verifies particle suspension, not field direction balance.
Part weight has nothing to do with field verification.

content.stem: A shaft is suspected of having transverse fatigue cracks. The preferred magnetization is:
content.explanation: Transverse cracks lie across the axis, so a longitudinal field (coil) that runs along the axis crosses them and reveals them best.
distractors: A circular head shot finds axial cracks, not transverse ones.
Residual alone may lack sensitivity; technique aside, field direction must suit transverse defects.
Magnetization is always required for MT.

content.stem: A bar is suspected of seams running along its length. The preferred magnetization is:
content.explanation: Longitudinal/axial seams run along the bar, so a circular field that encircles the bar crosses them and gives the best indications.
distractors: A coil's longitudinal field runs along the seams and would miss them.
A yoke gives a longitudinal field, again poorly suited to axial seams.
Demagnetization is a finishing step, not the inspection field for axial seams.

content.stem: An electromagnetic yoke induces what type of field in the area between its poles?
content.explanation: A yoke acts like a horseshoe magnet, inducing a longitudinal field between its legs, ideal for detecting discontinuities transverse to the line connecting the poles.
distractors: Circular fields come from current through the part or a central conductor.
A toroidal field is the contained circular field of a ring, not a yoke field.
The yoke field runs between poles, not radially outward.

content.stem: To find discontinuities of all orientations in a small area with a yoke, the inspector should:
options: Make two passes with the yoke rotated about 90 degrees between them
Make a single pass in one direction
Apply maximum current in one pass
content.explanation: Because a yoke field is directional, the area is examined twice with the yoke rotated roughly perpendicular between passes so cracks of any orientation cross the field in one of the passes.
distractors: A single pass leaves cracks parallel to that field undetected.
Increasing current does not change the single-direction limitation of one pass.
Two perpendicular passes, not residual technique, address orientation coverage with a yoke.

content.stem: An AC yoke should be capable of lifting at least what weight at its maximum pole spacing, as a field-adequacy check?
content.explanation: A common field-strength check requires an AC yoke to lift 10 lb and a DC (or permanent-magnet) yoke to lift 40 lb at the spacing to be used.
distractors: 40 lb is the lift requirement for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke, not AC.
1 lb is far below the required AC yoke lift.
100 lb exceeds the standard lift-test requirement for either yoke type.

content.stem: A DC or permanent-magnet yoke should be capable of lifting at least:
content.explanation: The lift test for DC and permanent-magnet yokes is 40 lb, reflecting the stronger field needed; AC yokes are checked at 10 lb.
distractors: 10 lb is the AC yoke requirement.
5 lb is below the requirement for either yoke type.
A lift test is a standard adequacy check and does apply.

content.stem: Induced-current magnetization is particularly useful for:
options: Ring-shaped parts, to find circumferential discontinuities without contact
Long solid shafts needing axial cracks found
content.explanation: Induced-current (toroidal) magnetization circulates current in a ring-shaped part by transformer action, producing a circumferential current and a field that reveals circumferential discontinuities without electrical contact.
distractors: Long solid shafts are better served by head shots or coils, not induced-current toroidal setups.
Flat plate is typically handled by yokes or prods, not induced current.
Induced current is a magnetizing method, not a demagnetizing one.

content.stem: A 'quick break' feature in a magnetizing circuit improves detection of which discontinuities?
options: Those near the ends of a part magnetized longitudinally
Subsurface inclusions deep in the part
content.explanation: Rapidly collapsing the current induces eddy effects that strengthen the field near the ends of longitudinally magnetized parts, improving end-region detection where the field would otherwise be weak.
distractors: Quick break is not specific to inside-diameter cracks.
It does not target deep subsurface inclusions.
It aids end-region detection, not specifically mid-length transverse cracks.

content.stem: Coil magnetization formulas based on L/D require that the part's length-to-diameter ratio be at least:
content.explanation: Standard coil ampere-turn formulas apply for L/D from about 2 to 15. For L/D below 2, the part is effectively too short; pole pieces or an effective-length adjustment are used.
distractors: L/D of 10 is within range but is not the minimum limit.
An L/D of 0.5 is far too low for the standard formulas.
L/D of 25 exceeds the usual upper bound of about 15 for the formulas.

content.stem: When a part is too short (L/D less than 2) for coil magnetization, a common remedy is to:
options: Add ferromagnetic pole pieces to effectively lengthen it
Switch to the residual technique automatically
content.explanation: Magnetically attaching pole pieces (or stacking like parts) raises the effective L/D so the longitudinal field can be established adequately.
distractors: Overheating the part is unsafe and does not fix the L/D limitation.
Changing to residual does not resolve a short-part longitudinal-field problem.
Switching methods abandons MT rather than solving the coil setup.

content.stem: For maximum sensitivity in a low-fill-factor coil shot, a long part should be:
options: Placed against the inside wall of the coil and inspected in sections
Centered in the coil and inspected once
content.explanation: The effective field of a coil extends only about 9 in beyond each end of the coil. A long part is placed against the coil's inner wall and inspected in overlapping sections.
distractors: Centering a long part inspects only the central region in one shot, leaving the ends underfield.
Holding the part outside the coil removes it from the effective field.
Continuous rotation does not address the limited longitudinal extent of the coil field.

content.stem: The effective longitudinal field of a coil extends approximately how far beyond each side of the coil?
options: The full length of any part
content.explanation: Useful field reaches only about 9 in past each end of the coil, which is why long parts are inspected in sections. A separate rule of thumb sizes the effective region to the coil itself; the two heuristics are not the same and should not be treated as equivalent.
distractors: The field does not reach as far as 3 ft beyond the coil.
It does not cover the full length of long parts in one position.
The effective field extends somewhat beyond the winding, not only inside it.

content.stem: Prods and yokes are best described as providing:
options: Circular fields throughout the entire part
content.explanation: Prods and yokes magnetize only the region between their contacts/poles, so large parts are covered by many overlapping placements.
distractors: Neither magnetizes a large whole part uniformly in one shot.
A yoke produces a longitudinal local field; a prod produces a local circular field, not a whole-part circular field.
Both are normally used with the continuous technique, not residual only.

content.stem: Copper braid or lead pads are placed on head/tailstock contacts mainly to:
options: Ensure good electrical contact and reduce arc burns/heat at the part ends
content.explanation: Conductive contact pads spread current and improve contact, reducing the local heating and arc-burn risk at the clamping points.
distractors: Contact pads do not change the material's retentivity.
Bath filtering is unrelated to contact pads.
UV shielding is a lighting concern, not a function of contact pads.

content.stem: If a complex part is given a head shot, regions that carry little or no current will:
options: Receive little circular field and may be inadequately inspected
content.explanation: The circular field follows the current. Branches or features that carry little current get a weak field, so additional shots or alternate methods are needed to cover them.
distractors: Low-current regions get weak fields and weak indications, not the strongest.
Low current does not demagnetize a region.
Field strength does not create cracks.

content.stem: A disadvantage of direct-contact (head shot, prod) methods on finished parts is:
options: Possible contact marking or arc burn at the electrodes
Inability to find any surface cracks
content.explanation: Direct-contact methods can mark or burn finished surfaces at the electrodes, so non-contact methods (coil, central conductor) are preferred on critical finished parts.
distractors: Direct methods are very capable of finding surface cracks.
MT requires ferromagnetic material regardless of method.
Current must always be controlled; that is not an advantage of these methods.

content.stem: Using a central conductor, the field on the bore wall is adequate for inspection out to roughly:
options: Four times the conductor diameter around the conductor
The full bore regardless of size
content.explanation: With an offset conductor, only the bore region within about four conductor diameters has adequate field, so the part is rotated to inspect the full circumference in overlapping passes.
distractors: A non-filling conductor does not field the full bore uniformly in one position.
Coverage extends to about four conductor diameters, more than just one.
Ten times the bore diameter overstates the adequately fielded region.

content.stem: A typical complete inspection of a shaft for both axial and transverse cracks uses:
options: A circular shot and a longitudinal shot
content.explanation: Axial cracks need a circular field and transverse cracks need a longitudinal field, so both shots are performed to cover all orientations.
distractors: A single circular shot misses transverse cracks.
A single longitudinal shot misses axial cracks.
Demagnetization does not detect anything.

content.stem: In wet continuous magnetic particle testing, the correct sequence is to:
options: Flow the bath over the part, stop the flow, then apply the current shot
Apply the current first, then flow bath after current is off
Apply developer, then bath, then current
content.explanation: In wet continuous practice the bath is flowed to wet the surface, flow is stopped, and the magnetizing shot(s) are applied while particles are present so indications form, then current is removed.
distractors: Flowing bath only after current is off is the residual approach, not wet continuous.
Developer is a penetrant-testing material, not used in MT.
Demagnetizing before applying bath would remove the field needed to form indications.

content.stem: In the dry continuous technique, magnetic powder is:
options: Applied as a gentle cloud while the current is on, with excess blown off under current
Applied only after the current is off
Mixed into water and flowed on
Applied before the part is magnetized and left undisturbed
content.explanation: Dry powder is dusted on while the field is energized and the excess is removed with a gentle air stream while current remains on, so mobile particles can migrate to leakage fields.
distractors: Applying powder only after current is off is the residual approach.
Mixing powder in water describes the wet method, not dry.
Powder must be applied with the field on and excess removed under current for the continuous technique.

content.stem: When choosing between two perpendicular shots, the inspector should ensure that:
options: Each shot's field is adequate for the discontinuities it is meant to find
Both shots use identical current values
Only the stronger shot is recorded
The part is demagnetized between every particle application
content.explanation: Each direction must independently provide an adequate field (verified by indicators) for the orientation of discontinuity it targets; current values often differ between circular and longitudinal shots.
distractors: Circular and longitudinal shots usually require different current values, so identical values are not the goal.
Indications from both directions are evaluated, not just the stronger shot.
Demagnetizing between applications would defeat the inspection.

content.stem: For a steel pipe, the central conductor technique is preferred over a head shot mainly because it:
options: Magnetizes ID and OD without contact and avoids arc burns
content.explanation: The central conductor fields both surfaces of a hollow part without electrode contact, eliminating arc-burn risk and inspecting the inside diameter that a head shot reaches poorly.
distractors: It still requires current through the conductor.
It detects surface (and some subsurface) discontinuities, not only subsurface.
MT applies to ferromagnetic pipe; nonferromagnetic pipe cannot be inspected by MT.

content.stem: Which method generally allows the highest, most uniform circular field in a solid cylindrical part?
options: Direct head shot through the part
content.explanation: A direct head shot drives current through the full cross section, producing a strong, uniform circular field at the surface, ideal for axial discontinuities in solid cylinders.
distractors: A yoke gives a local longitudinal field, not a uniform circular field through a cylinder.
Powder without current provides no magnetizing field at all.
A residual field from a coil is longitudinal and generally weaker, not a strong circular field.

content.stem: Increasing the number of turns in a coil, with current held constant, will:
options: Have no effect on the field
content.explanation: MMF equals ampere-turns (N x I). More turns at the same current raises the ampere-turns and thus the longitudinal field.
distractors: More turns increase, not decrease, the field for constant current.
Turns directly affect ampere-turns, so there is an effect.
Reversing direction requires reversing current, not adding turns.

content.stem: Large irregular castings with many surfaces are most practically inspected using:
options: Prods and/or yokes applied in overlapping local areas
A single coil shot for the whole casting
content.explanation: Prods and yokes magnetize local areas, so large complex castings are covered by systematic overlapping placements with attention to two field directions per area.
distractors: A single coil shot cannot uniformly field a large irregular casting.
A central conductor applies to hollow parts with a bore, not general castings.
Residual technique still requires magnetizing equipment and is poorly suited to large soft castings.

content.stem: In the continuous technique, the magnetizing current is typically applied for:
options: A short duration (about 0.5 s or more) while particles are present, often as repeated shots
content.explanation: The continuous technique uses brief energizations (commonly two or more shots of about half a second or more) while particles are present so indications can build; it is not a sustained multi-minute current.
distractors: Multi-minute continuous current would overheat the part and equipment.
A few microseconds is too brief to allow particle migration and indication buildup.
Current is pulsed for inspection, not left on for an entire shift.

content.stem: Which statement about field direction is correct?
options: Circular fields find longitudinal defects; longitudinal fields find transverse defects
Circular fields find transverse defects; longitudinal fields find longitudinal defects
Both field types find the same defects equally
Field direction does not affect detection
content.explanation: Indications form across the field. A circular field (encircling the part) crosses longitudinal/axial defects; a longitudinal field (along the part) crosses transverse defects.
distractors: This reverses the correct relationship between field type and defect orientation.
The two field types preferentially find perpendicular defect orientations, not the same ones.
Field direction is the central factor in MT detectability.

content.stem: Alternating current (AC) magnetization concentrates the field:
options: At and near the surface of the part
Uniformly through the full cross section
content.explanation: Because of the skin effect, AC confines current and field to a thin surface layer, making AC excellent for surface discontinuities but poor for subsurface ones.
distractors: AC does not penetrate deeply; that is a characteristic of DC.
AC fields are present along the part, not only at the ends.
Uniform full-section field is more characteristic of DC than AC.

content.stem: The 'skin effect' associated with AC refers to the tendency of current to:
options: Flow mainly near the surface of a conductor
content.explanation: At AC frequencies, induced eddy effects push current toward the conductor surface, concentrating the magnetic field there.
distractors: The current concentrates at the surface, not the center.
Current still flows; it simply redistributes toward the surface.
The skin effect changes current distribution, not part polarity.

content.stem: Direct current (DC) is preferred over AC when the goal is to detect:
content.explanation: DC penetrates more deeply than AC, producing field below the surface, so it is better for subsurface discontinuities. AC excels at surface defects.
distractors: AC is generally superior for the finest surface cracks due to surface concentration and particle mobility.
Neither current detects defects on nonmagnetic parts; MT needs ferromagnetism.
All MT requires a magnetizing field.

content.stem: Full-wave rectified AC (FWDC) behaves most like:
options: Direct current, giving good subsurface penetration
Pure AC with strong skin effect
content.explanation: FWDC has low ripple and behaves much like straight DC, giving good penetration for subsurface discontinuities while being derived from an AC supply.
distractors: FWDC has reduced AC character and does not show a strong skin effect like pure AC.
FWDC produces a strong, steady field, not the absence of one.
FWDC is a rectified current source, not a permanent magnet.

content.stem: Half-wave rectified AC (HWDC) is especially favored for:
options: Dry-powder inspection, because its pulsation gives particles mobility
content.explanation: HWDC has a strong pulsating component that agitates dry powder, improving particle mobility and subsurface sensitivity, making it a common choice with dry powder on castings and welds.
distractors: HWDC is not specific to wet fluorescent; its pulsation benefits dry powder mobility.
HWDC is a magnetizing current, not a demagnetizing method.
Nonferromagnetic parts cannot be inspected by MT regardless of current.

content.stem: The pulsating nature of half-wave DC aids dry-powder inspection by:
options: Giving the powder mobility so it can migrate to leakage fields
Reducing the field to zero between pulses permanently
content.explanation: The pulsing field repeatedly nudges dry particles, helping them move across the surface and collect at leakage fields, which improves sensitivity to weak and subsurface indications.
distractors: The benefit is mechanical mobility, not heating.
Particles are moved magnetically, not by electrostatic charging from the pulsation.
The field pulses but is not permanently reduced to zero; it cycles.

content.stem: Rank the following by increasing subsurface penetration capability:
content.explanation: AC is shallowest (surface only), HWDC penetrates somewhat with strong pulsation, and FWDC/DC penetrate deepest, so increasing penetration runs AC, HWDC, FWDC/DC.
distractors: This reverses the order; DC penetrates more than AC, not less.
AC is the least penetrating, so it cannot sit in the middle of an increasing list.
Penetration differs markedly among the current types.

content.stem: For very fine surface cracks, AC often outperforms DC because:
options: The AC field concentrates at the surface and the pulsation improves particle mobility
AC eliminates the need for two field directions
content.explanation: AC keeps field energy at the surface and its rapid polarity reversals (120 per second on a 60 Hz supply) aid particle movement, sharpening fine surface indications. DC drives energy below the surface where fine surface cracks gain less.
distractors: AC penetrates less, not more, than DC.
Two directions are still required regardless of current type.
No current can magnetize a nonmagnetic part.

content.stem: For the residual technique, which current generally leaves the strongest residual field in a retentive part?
content.explanation: DC magnetizes the full cross section and leaves a strong, stable residual field in retentive materials. AC, reversing rapidly, tends to leave a weaker and less predictable residual field.
distractors: AC leaves a weak, direction-uncertain residual field, poor for residual inspection.
Residual inspection still requires a prior magnetizing current.
Minimum-output HWDC would not maximize residual field.

content.stem: AC is well suited to demagnetization because it:
options: Naturally reverses direction each cycle, allowing decreasing reversals
Penetrates the deepest of all currents
content.explanation: AC reverses 120 times per second, so reducing its amplitude while the part withdraws (or stepping it down) drives residual flux toward zero. Its limited penetration, however, can leave deep residual fields in thick parts.
distractors: AC reverses continuously; that is exactly why it demagnetizes well.
AC penetrates the least, not the most.
AC amplitude is readily reduced, which is the basis of AC demagnetization.

content.stem: For demagnetizing thick parts with deep residual fields, reversing DC of decreasing amplitude is preferred over AC because:
options: DC penetrates deeply enough to reach and reduce the interior field
DC cannot be reduced in steps
content.explanation: AC's shallow penetration may not reach a deep residual field, so reversing-and-decreasing DC, which penetrates the section, is used to demagnetize thick parts.
distractors: AC penetrates less than DC, the reason it can fail on thick parts.
Reversing DC does reverse by design during demagnetization.
DC amplitude is stepped down during demagnetization.

content.stem: The magnetizing current value used in MT setups is most directly read from:
content.explanation: An ammeter indicates the magnetizing current applied. Field at the surface can be checked separately with a gaussmeter or indicators.
distractors: A gaussmeter reads tangential field strength in gauss, not the applied current.
A settling tube measures particle concentration, not current.
A light meter measures UV or white-light intensity, not current.

content.stem: For the same ammeter reading, AC will typically produce a surface field that is:
options: Stronger at the immediate surface than DC
Weaker at the surface than DC
content.explanation: Because AC concentrates at the surface, the immediate-surface field can be higher than DC for the same current, even though DC has more subsurface field.
distractors: AC is not weaker at the surface; it is concentrated there.
The distributions differ, so they are not identical everywhere.
AC produces a strong surface field, not zero.

content.stem: Rectification in an MT power supply converts:
options: AC line power into direct or pulsed DC for magnetization
content.explanation: Rectifiers turn AC mains into FWDC or HWDC, giving the penetration characteristics of DC while running from an AC supply.
distractors: Rectification produces DC from AC, not the reverse.
Rectification changes the current waveform, not converts current into voltage.
Rectifiers process electrical current, not magnetic field.

content.stem: Compared with full-wave DC, half-wave DC has:
content.explanation: Half-wave DC passes only half of each AC cycle, leaving a strongly pulsating waveform (high ripple). Full-wave DC is smoother, closer to steady DC.
distractors: Half-wave has more ripple than full-wave, not less.
Half-wave is highly pulsating, far from ripple-free.
Half-wave DC does not reverse polarity; it is unidirectional pulsing.

content.stem: AC is a good choice for thin-walled parts when the discontinuities of interest are:
content.explanation: AC's surface concentration suits surface-breaking discontinuities, which on thin parts are the dominant concern.
distractors: Deep subsurface inclusions favor DC penetration, not AC.
Nonmagnetic material cannot be inspected by MT.
AC field is at the surface, not concentrated at the center.

content.stem: Half-wave DC with dry powder is a classic combination for:
options: Detecting subsurface discontinuities in castings and weldments
content.explanation: HWDC penetration plus dry-powder mobility is well suited to the relatively rough surfaces and subsurface discontinuities common in castings and welds.
distractors: MT detects discontinuities in the ferromagnetic material, not defects in a paint layer.
Nonferrous parts are not ferromagnetic and cannot be inspected by MT.
HWDC is a magnetizing current, not a demagnetizing method.

content.stem: Excessively high magnetizing current can cause:
options: Part overheating and arc burns at contacts
Conversion of the part to nonmagnetic
content.explanation: Too much current heats the part, risks arc burns at electrodes, and produces heavy particle background, so current is set to provide adequate field without excess.
distractors: Beyond saturation, more current adds little detection benefit and increases problems.
High current magnetizes; it does not demagnetize.
Current does not change the part's intrinsic magnetic nature.

content.stem: A current waveform that is unidirectional but drops to zero 60 times per second is:
content.explanation: Half-wave rectification passes one polarity and blocks the other, so the current pulses to zero each cycle while remaining unidirectional.
distractors: Full-wave DC does not drop fully to zero each half cycle; it is smoother.
Pure AC reverses polarity rather than staying unidirectional.
Steady battery DC is constant and does not pulse to zero.

content.stem: For AC, increasing the frequency would, in general:
content.explanation: Higher frequency strengthens the skin effect, pushing field even closer to the surface and reducing penetration depth.
distractors: Higher frequency reduces, not increases, penetration.
Frequency clearly affects penetration through the skin effect.
Higher frequency intensifies the skin effect rather than eliminating it.

content.stem: Which current type, with wet fluorescent particles, gives the highest sensitivity to fine surface cracks?
content.explanation: AC with wet fluorescent bath maximizes fine surface-crack sensitivity due to surface field concentration and particle mobility from the reversals.
distractors: Full-wave DC drives field subsurface, reducing the edge on the finest surface cracks.
Half-wave DC favors dry powder and subsurface work, not the finest wet surface cracks.
Steady DC penetrates and is not optimal for the finest surface cracks.

content.stem: Which current type gives the best subsurface sensitivity?
content.explanation: Full-wave or steady DC penetrates deepest, giving the best subsurface leakage and detection.
distractors: AC is confined near the surface and is poor for subsurface defects.
Even low-frequency AC penetrates less than DC.
MT requires a magnetizing current.

content.stem: A part magnetized with AC and then checked residually often shows weak or inconsistent indications because:
options: AC may leave the part in a low or uncertain residual state when interrupted
content.explanation: AC reverses continuously and, depending on where in the cycle it is interrupted, can leave little or unpredictable residual field, so AC is generally not used for the residual technique.
distractors: AC does not reliably leave the part saturated; the residual state is uncertain.
AC penetrates shallowly, not too deeply.
AC does magnetize ferromagnetic parts; it just leaves poor residual fields.

content.stem: Reversing the direction of the magnetizing current in a head shot will:
options: Reverse the direction of the circular field
Change a circular field into a longitudinal one
content.explanation: The circular field direction follows the current per the right-hand rule, so reversing current reverses the field direction while keeping it circular.
distractors: Reversing current does not change the field type, only its direction.
Reversing current does not remove the field.
Current direction has no effect on the part material.

content.stem: Why is steady battery-type DC seldom used for routine high-current MT?
options: Practical high magnetizing currents are more easily produced by rectified line power
content.explanation: The high amperages required are produced economically by rectifying line power (FWDC/HWDC); large batteries are impractical for the sustained high currents of MT.
distractors: Steady DC actually penetrates well; practicality, not penetration, is the issue.
Battery DC is unidirectional and does not reverse polarity.
DC readily magnetizes steel; the limitation is supplying the needed current.

content.stem: Compared with low-voltage rectified DC supplies, the magnetizing circuits in MT generally operate at:
content.explanation: MT magnetizing circuits use low voltage with very high current (hundreds to thousands of amperes) to establish strong fields, which is why heavy cables and good contacts matter.
distractors: MT uses high current at low voltage, not high voltage at low current.
Voltages are kept low; it is the current that is high.
Substantial current is required to magnetize parts.

content.stem: Three-phase full-wave rectified current is valued because it provides:
options: A smooth, high-output DC with low ripple for deep penetration
content.explanation: Three-phase FWDC delivers smooth high-current DC with minimal ripple, giving strong, deep, uniform fields suited to subsurface inspection of large parts.
distractors: Three-phase FWDC has low ripple, unlike pulsating half-wave.
Its penetration is deep, unlike the surface concentration of AC.
It is a magnetizing supply, not a demagnetizer.

content.stem: For surface cracks on a thin-walled steel tube using a central conductor, the current type often chosen is:
options: AC, for strong surface field and particle mobility
content.explanation: Surface cracks on thin walls are well served by AC's surface concentration; deep penetration is unnecessary, so AC with the central conductor is a common choice.
distractors: Deep penetration is not needed for surface cracks on thin walls.
Residual technique is less sensitive for fine surface cracks here.
Deep-inclusion sensitivity (HWDC) is not the goal for thin-wall surface cracks.

content.stem: As you move from the surface into the depth of a part magnetized with DC, the available field for detection generally:
options: Decreases with depth but reaches deeper than AC
Stays exactly constant to the core
Is always zero below the surface
content.explanation: Even with DC, leakage available at the surface from a discontinuity weakens with the defect's depth, but DC reaches deeper than AC, which is essentially surface-confined.
distractors: Detectable field does not grow with depth; deeper defects are harder to find.
Field and detectability are not constant all the way to the core.
DC does provide subsurface field, so it is not zero below the surface.

content.stem: Which pairing of current type and strength is correct?
options: AC: best surface sensitivity; FWDC/DC: best subsurface penetration
AC: best subsurface; DC: best surface only
content.explanation: AC excels at surface discontinuities; full-wave/steady DC excels at subsurface; HWDC bridges with strong pulsation and useful penetration, especially with dry powder.
distractors: This reverses the strengths of AC and DC.
AC and DC differ significantly in penetration and surface performance.
HWDC does penetrate; it is favored partly for subsurface work.

content.stem: The quick-break circuit improves end-region detection by rapidly:
options: Collapsing the magnetizing current to induce a stronger momentary field near the ends
Increasing the current slowly over several seconds
content.explanation: A fast current collapse induces transient eddy effects that momentarily strengthen the field at the ends of a longitudinally magnetized part, where the field is otherwise weak.
distractors: A slow increase does not produce the quick-break end-field benefit.
Quick break is a fast collapse, not continuous polarity reversal.
Quick break is an electrical feature, unrelated to bath concentration.

content.stem: A hardened steel bearing race (high retentivity) is to be inspected by the residual technique. Best magnetizing current:
options: DC or FWDC to establish a strong residual field
AC to leave a strong residual field
No current is needed for residual
content.explanation: The residual technique benefits from DC/FWDC, which fully magnetizes the section and leaves a strong, stable residual field in a retentive material.
distractors: AC tends to leave a weak, uncertain residual field.
A magnetizing current is required before residual inspection.
Minimum HWDC would not maximize the residual field needed.

content.stem: Because of the skin effect, AC magnetic particle testing should not be relied upon to find:
content.explanation: AC fields do not penetrate, so AC cannot reliably reveal subsurface discontinuities; it is reserved for surface-breaking defects.
distractors: Surface-breaking cracks are exactly what AC finds best.
Fine surface porosity is detectable with AC at the surface.
Grinding cracks are surface-breaking and well suited to AC.

content.stem: Full-wave DC compared with AC, for the residual technique, generally:
options: Leaves a stronger and more usable residual field
content.explanation: FWDC magnetizes the full section and leaves a strong residual field in retentive parts, making it preferred over AC for residual inspection.
distractors: FWDC leaves a stronger, not weaker, residual field than AC.
FWDC does leave a residual field in retentive material.
FWDC magnetizes the part effectively.

content.stem: Applying two or more brief shots in the continuous technique is done to:
options: Ensure particles have reached leakage fields while the field is on
Heat the part to improve contrast
Reduce the field below detection threshold
content.explanation: Multiple short shots while particles are present give them repeated opportunity to migrate and build indications at leakage fields before current is removed.
distractors: Brief on-shots magnetize; they do not demagnetize.
The purpose is particle migration, not heating for contrast.
The shots maintain an adequate field, not reduce it below threshold.

content.stem: A common bench demagnetizer is an AC coil through which the part is:
options: Passed and slowly withdrawn to a distance while the coil is energized
Held stationary at full current indefinitely
content.explanation: Passing the part through an energized AC coil and withdrawing it several feet lets the part experience diminishing reversing fields, demagnetizing it.
distractors: Holding the part at full current in the coil magnetizes rather than demagnetizes it.
Bath immersion is unrelated to AC-coil demagnetization.
Mechanical shock is not the demagnetization mechanism here.

content.stem: A forging may contain inclusions about 0.060 in below the surface. The most suitable current is:
content.explanation: Subsurface inclusions need penetration, so full-wave DC (often with dry powder or wet bath at adequate field) is appropriate; AC would not reach them.
distractors: AC is surface-confined and would miss subsurface inclusions.
Current type strongly affects subsurface detection.
Residual technique is generally less sensitive for such subsurface defects.

content.stem: Standard line-frequency AC used in MT in North America is:
content.explanation: MT AC equipment typically runs at the 60 Hz line frequency (50 Hz in many other regions), which provides the surface concentration and reversals used for surface inspection and demagnetization.
distractors: 400 Hz is used in some aircraft power systems but is not standard MT line frequency.
5 Hz is not a standard line frequency for MT.
AC by definition is not direct current.

content.stem: When using prods, lower arc-burn risk is associated with:
options: Maintaining firm contact and not breaking contact under current
Using the highest possible current always
Lifting a prod while current flows
content.explanation: Arc burns come from breaking or making contact under current or poor contact. Firm contact and breaking the circuit before lifting prods reduce the risk regardless of current type.
distractors: Always using the highest current increases heating and arc-burn risk.
Lifting a prod under current is a primary cause of arc burns.
Shorting prods together under load can cause arcing and is unsafe.

content.stem: Which is the best general guideline for choosing current type?
options: AC for surface defects; DC/FWDC for subsurface; HWDC with dry powder for rough/subsurface work
content.explanation: Match the current to the task: AC for surface, FWDC/DC for subsurface, and HWDC with dry powder for rough surfaces and subsurface defects on castings and welds.
distractors: AC is poor for subsurface defects, so it is not universally best.
DC is less ideal than AC for the finest surface cracks, so it is not universally best.
Current type is a key variable affecting detection.

content.stem: A wet horizontal ('bench') unit typically provides which magnetizing capabilities?
options: Head shot (circular) and coil (longitudinal) in one machine
content.explanation: A wet horizontal unit has head/tailstock contacts for circular shots and a built-in coil for longitudinal shots, plus bath application and demagnetization, making it a versatile bench machine.
distractors: Bench units do far more than yoke magnetization.
Wet horizontal units apply wet bath, not just dry powder.
They magnetize and inspect, not only demagnetize.

content.stem: An electromagnetic yoke is most accurately described as a:
options: Portable device producing a local longitudinal field between two poles
content.explanation: The yoke is a portable horseshoe electromagnet that produces a local longitudinal field between its legs, used for field inspection of welds and local areas.
distractors: A yoke is portable and produces a longitudinal, not circular, field.
A yoke magnetizes; it does not agitate bath.
A yoke is a magnetizer, not a lighting device.

content.stem: Articulated (hinged) legs on a yoke are provided to:
options: Allow good pole contact on irregular or curved surfaces
Eliminate the need for two directions
content.explanation: Hinged legs let both poles seat on uneven or curved surfaces, maintaining a good magnetic circuit and field across the area of interest.
distractors: Leg articulation does not affect bath concentration.
Articulation is mechanical and unrelated to UV output.
Two perpendicular passes are still required regardless of leg articulation.

content.stem: Prod assemblies typically include which safety-relevant feature?
options: A remote (trigger) switch so current flows only when intended
An automatic demagnetizer on each tip
content.explanation: Prods use a trigger/remote switch so current is applied only when the prods are firmly placed, reducing arc-burn risk from making or breaking contact under load.
distractors: Prods are magnetizing tools and do not include UV lamps.
Concentration measurement is done with a settling tube, not at the prods.
Prods do not carry per-tip demagnetizers.

content.stem: A fixed multi-turn coil on a bench unit is used to produce:
options: A longitudinal field for transverse-defect detection
A circular field for axial defects
content.explanation: The coil establishes a longitudinal field along parts placed in or against it, revealing transverse discontinuities.
distractors: Circular fields for axial defects come from head shots or central conductors, not the coil.
The coil magnetizes; it does not circulate bath.
The coil is not a light source.

content.stem: A central conductor is typically a:
options: Solid or hollow copper bar passed through the bore of a hollow part
content.explanation: A copper (or aluminum) conductor bar is threaded through the bore and carries the magnetizing current, fielding the inside and outside surfaces of hollow parts.
distractors: A coil around the part is a different (longitudinal) setup.
A central conductor carries current; it is not a permanent magnet.
It is a conductor, not a lighting device.

content.stem: The ammeter on an MT unit is used to:
options: Set and verify the magnetizing current
content.explanation: The ammeter lets the operator set the required current and confirm it during the shot. Field strength is verified separately with indicators or a gaussmeter.
distractors: UV intensity is measured with a radiometer/light meter.
Bath concentration is measured with a settling tube.
Surface temperature is not what an ammeter reads.

content.stem: A pie-shaped (pie gauge) field indicator is used to:
options: Show field direction and the presence of an adequate field at the surface
Quantify exact field strength in gauss
Replace the need for two directions
content.explanation: The pie gauge, an eight-segment iron disk with a nonferrous face, shows the direction of the field and confirms a usable field is present, but it does not give a numeric field value.
distractors: The pie gauge is qualitative; it does not read exact gauss values.
It indicates magnetic field, not bath chemistry.
It helps confirm direction but does not eliminate the need for two-direction inspection.

content.stem: A QQI (quantitative quality indicator) shim is used to:
options: Verify that an adequate field exists at the part surface in the required direction(s)
content.explanation: QQI shims (artificial flaw shims) are attached to the part surface; the appearance of their etched flaw patterns confirms adequate field strength and direction at that location, including in multidirectional setups.
distractors: QQIs verify field, not ambient light, which a light meter measures.
QQIs are field verification tools, not demagnetizers.
QQIs do not filter bath.

content.stem: QQI shims are normally applied with the artificial-flaw side:
options: Against the part surface (flaw side down), bonded so flux must cross it
content.explanation: The shim is bonded flaw-side toward the part so the part's surface field crosses the etched pattern, producing indications only when the field is adequate and correctly oriented.
distractors: Facing the flaw away from the part would not let the part's field develop the pattern correctly.
QQIs are bonded to the part, not floated in bath.
QQIs go on the part surface, not inside the coil.

content.stem: A Hall-effect gaussmeter with a tangential probe measures:
options: The tangential (surface) magnetic field strength in gauss
content.explanation: A tangential-field Hall probe reads the field strength parallel to the surface in gauss, used to confirm field adequacy (often a target range such as 30 to 60 gauss at the surface).
distractors: Concentration is read with a settling tube, not a gaussmeter.
UV-A is measured with a radiometer.
Hardness is a mechanical property, not what a gaussmeter measures.

content.stem: A commonly cited adequate tangential field strength at the part surface for MT is approximately:
content.explanation: A tangential surface field on the order of 30 to 60 gauss is a frequently used adequacy guideline, confirmed with a Hall-effect gaussmeter.
distractors: 2 to 5 gauss is far below the field needed to reliably form indications.
300 to 600 gauss is well above the typical adequacy guideline.
Less than 1 gauss is near the demagnetized residual limit, not an inspection field.

content.stem: After demagnetization, residual field on a part is commonly verified with a:
options: Field indicator/gaussmeter showing the residual is below an acceptance limit
Pie gauge held in the bath
content.explanation: A residual field meter or gaussmeter confirms the leftover field is below the specified limit (for example, a few gauss), ensuring demagnetization is adequate.
distractors: A pie gauge indicates active fields qualitatively, not a low residual value, and is not used in the bath this way.
A settling tube measures particle concentration, not residual field.
A white-light meter measures illumination, not magnetic field.

content.stem: The lamp used for fluorescent magnetic particle inspection emits primarily:
content.explanation: Fluorescent MT uses UV-A near 365 nm to excite the fluorescent particles, which then emit visible light. UV-C is hazardous and not used for this purpose.
distractors: UV-C is germicidal and unsafe for inspection use; it is not the MT lamp.
Infrared does not excite the fluorescent dyes.
Visible blue light alone does not provide the UV-A excitation needed.

content.stem: Minimum UV-A irradiance at the part surface for fluorescent MT is commonly specified as:
content.explanation: A minimum UV-A irradiance of 1000 microwatts/cm-squared at the examination surface is the common requirement for fluorescent MT, verified with a radiometer.
distractors: 100 microwatts/cm-squared is below the standard minimum for fluorescent MT.
10 microwatts/cm-squared is far too low.
1 microwatt/cm-squared is negligible for exciting fluorescent particles.

content.stem: During fluorescent MT, ambient (white) light in the inspection area should not exceed about:
content.explanation: Ambient white light is kept low, commonly at or below 2 foot-candles (about 20 lux), so faint fluorescent indications are visible.
distractors: 100 foot-candles is a minimum for visible (non-fluorescent) inspection, not a fluorescent ambient limit.
